notes.b: A socio-economic region is defined by its level of wealth and development, judged by several indicators at once.
points: The indicators include income or GDP per head, unemployment, the mix of primary, secondary and tertiary jobs, migration, age structure, education and services.
Primary jobs take materials from the land and sea (farming, fishing, forestry, mining); secondary jobs make goods in factories; tertiary jobs provide services.
The core–periphery idea: wealth, people and investment concentrate in a core, while the periphery loses people and capital to it.
Cumulative causation: each advantage in the core attracts more, so the gap tends to widen unless governments or the EU intervene.

notes.b: A core region has a strong, growing economy, high incomes, and a concentration of population, investment and decision-making.
points: High GDP per head and low unemployment.
A large tertiary (services) sector, including finance, company headquarters and high-tech industry.
Most foreign investment goes to the core.
Net in-migration of young, educated workers gives it a young population.
Dense, well-developed infrastructure: motorways, airports, ports and rail lines.
Universities and research institutions, and usually the capital city with the seat of government.
Causes: accessibility, a large market and labour force, an early start, government and capital functions, and agglomeration, where firms attract more firms to the same place.
Problems of success: congestion, high house prices, urban sprawl and pressure on services.
Greater Dublin Area: Dublin, Kildare, Meath and Wicklow. County Dublin had about 1.45 million people in Census 2022.
Dublin, the capital, has the seat of government, and its docklands host the European headquarters of many technology firms, e.g. Google. The Irish core is covered in the Irish Regions chapter.
Paris Basin, France: its region, Île-de-France, has about 12 million people. The Paris Basin is covered in the European Regions chapter.
The Blue Banana: the curved belt of Europe's main core, running from south-east England and London through the Benelux countries and the Rhine valley to northern Italy (Milan).

notes.b: A peripheral region is distant, physically or economically, from the core, with a weaker economy and fewer opportunities.
points: Remote location and poor access to markets and services.
Difficult physical conditions: mountains, high rainfall, poor soils and a short growing season.
Dependence on primary activity: small farms, fishing and forestry.
Low incomes and higher unemployment or underemployment.
Net out-migration of young adults, leaving an ageing population and falling numbers in rural areas.
Fewer services, and small, scattered settlements.
EU regional and cohesion funds and state agencies channel investment into the periphery.
Better roads and broadband, and decentralisation of government offices, help peripheral areas keep people and jobs.
Tourism builds on the scenery and culture of peripheral areas.
The case-study chapters give the detail for each example.
West of Ireland: the Northern and Western regional assembly area. Co. Leitrim has the smallest population of any Irish county.
The Mezzogiorno, southern Italy, is covered in the European Regions chapter.
Northern Norway: Arctic, remote and reliant on fishing.
North-west Scotland: the Highlands and Islands.
A less-developed region is one whose level of development is well below the national or EU average.
In EU regional policy, a less-developed region has GDP per head below 75% of the EU average, and receives the most EU aid.
Most less-developed regions in Europe are also peripheral: the Mezzogiorno, and much of eastern Europe such as Romania and Bulgaria.
Peripheral is not the same as less-developed: a peripheral region can lie in a rich country, such as the West of Ireland or northern Norway.
Ireland was a single Objective 1 region until 1999. From 2000 to 2006 only the BMW (Border, Midland and Western) region kept Objective 1 status.
At a global scale, less-developed regions are developing countries. India is the continental example, covered in its own chapter.
The Mezzogiorno's development history, beginning with the Cassa per il Mezzogiorno (Fund for the South) in 1950, is covered in the European Regions chapter.

notes.b: A region of industrial decline grew on heavy, traditional industry and has since lost much of it.
points: Its traditional industries include coal mining, iron and steel, shipbuilding and textiles.
Causes: coal seams exhausted or too costly to work; cheaper imports and competition from newly industrialised countries.
Further causes: coal replaced by oil and gas; out-of-date plant; and automation, which needs fewer workers.
Effects: high unemployment, especially among older male workers; derelict factories, mines and spoil heaps; and polluted land.
Further effects: out-migration, falling services, and a poor image that deters new investment.

Responses: retraining; clearing and cleaning derelict land; attracting new light industry and services; universities and technology parks; reuse of industrial heritage for tourism and culture; EU funds.
Sambre–Meuse valley, Wallonia, Belgium: coal mining and steel along the Sambre and Meuse, e.g. Charleroi on the Sambre and Liège on the Meuse.
Ruhr, Germany (North Rhine-Westphalia): Europe's largest coal and steel region, with cities including Essen, Dortmund and Duisburg.
Prosper-Haniel in Bottrop, the last hard-coal mine in Germany, closed in 2018. The Zollverein coal mine complex in Essen became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001 and is now a cultural centre.
South Wales coalfield, including the Rhondda valleys: coal mining collapsed in the late 20th century.
Nord–Pas-de-Calais, France, is a further European example.
Belfast: the Harland and Wolff shipyard, which built the Titanic (launched 1911), declined greatly in the late 20th century.

Dublin docklands: port jobs fell with containerisation. The International Financial Services Centre (IFSC), established in 1987 on derelict dockland, regenerated the area. Irish economic evidence is in the Primary, Secondary and Tertiary Economic Activities chapter.
Primary: large, commercial, efficient farms on good land in the core; small, fragmented farms on poor land in the periphery, with more fishing and forestry.
Secondary: concentrations of manufacturing and multinational investment in the core; few, small and often grant-aided factories in the periphery.
Tertiary: finance, headquarters, government, universities, and major ports and airports in the core; tourism and public services in the periphery.

keyTerms.definition: A region defined by its level of wealth and development, judged by several indicators together.
A region with a strong, growing economy and a concentration of population, investment and decision-making.
A region distant, physically or economically, from the core, with a weaker economy and fewer opportunities.
The process by which advantages in a core attract further growth, widening the gap with the periphery.
A region whose development is well below the national or EU average; in EU policy, GDP per head below 75% of the EU average.
A region that grew on heavy, traditional industry and has since lost much of it.
The clustering of firms in one place, which attracts more firms because of shared markets, labour and services.

factCards.definition: Core: the Paris Basin, the Greater Dublin Area. Peripheral: the West of Ireland, the BMW region, the Mezzogiorno, northern Norway. Industrial decline: the Sambre–Meuse valley, the Ruhr, the South Wales coalfield.

factCards.term: The Ruhr: key facts as a region of industrial decline

factCards.definition: Belfast: the Harland and Wolff shipyard, which built the Titanic (launched 1911), declined greatly in the late 20th century. Dublin docklands: port jobs fell with containerisation; the IFSC, set up in 1987 on derelict dockland, regenerated the area.

factCards.term: Core vs peripheral regions: how economic activity differs
factCards.definition: Primary: large commercial farms on good land vs small, fragmented farms on poor land. Secondary: manufacturing and multinational investment vs few small, often grant-aided factories. Tertiary: finance, headquarters, government vs tourism, public services.

questions.prompt: Contrast the primary, secondary and tertiary activities of a core region and a peripheral region you have studied.
questions.model: Primary: core regions have large, commercial, efficient farms on good land, while the West of Ireland periphery has small, fragmented farms on poor land, with more fishing and forestry. Secondary: the core attracts manufacturing and multinational investment, while the periphery has few, small and often grant-aided factories. Tertiary: the core has finance, company headquarters, government, universities, and major ports and airports, while the periphery depends on tourism and public services. Causes: the core's accessibility, large market and labour force, and agglomeration draw investment in; the periphery's remoteness, difficult physical conditions and out-migration of young adults keep it weak. Effects: the core has congestion, high house prices and urban sprawl, while the periphery has an ageing population, falling rural numbers and fewer services. Responses in the periphery include EU regional and cohesion funds, better roads and broadband, and tourism.

questions.prompt: Examine the causes and effects of industrial decline in a region you have studied.
questions.model: Example: the Ruhr in western Germany. It was Europe's largest coal and steel region, with cities including Essen, Dortmund and Duisburg. Causes: coal seams became exhausted or too costly to work; cheaper imports and competition from newly industrialised countries; coal was replaced by oil and gas; plant was out of date; and automation needed fewer workers. Effects: high unemployment, especially among older male workers; derelict factories, mines and spoil heaps; polluted land; out-migration; falling services; and a poor image that deters new investment. Responses: the last hard-coal mine, Prosper-Haniel in Bottrop, closed in 2018; the Zollverein coal mine complex in Essen, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2001, was converted into a cultural centre; derelict land was cleared and cleaned; new light industry, services, universities and technology parks were attracted; and EU funds supported retraining and renewal.

questions.prompt: Describe the main characteristics of (i) a core region and (ii) a peripheral region, naming an example of each.
questions.model: (i) Core region: strong, growing economy with high GDP per head and low unemployment; a large tertiary sector with finance, headquarters and high-tech industry; most foreign investment; net in-migration of young, educated workers; dense infrastructure of motorways, airports, ports and rail; universities; and usually the capital city. Example: the Greater Dublin Area (Dublin, Kildare, Meath and Wicklow), with County Dublin home to about 1.45 million people in Census 2022. (ii) Peripheral region: distant from the core with poor access; difficult physical conditions such as mountains, high rainfall and poor soils; dependence on small farms, fishing and forestry; low incomes and higher unemployment; net out-migration of young adults and an ageing population; fewer services and small, scattered settlements. Example: the West of Ireland, the Northern and Western regional assembly area.
